question: A number of reliable sources – including the Wall Street Journal – indicate that, according to official documents analysed by the US Department of Health, Chinese researchers had isolated and sequenced the SARS-CoV-2 virus as early as late December 2019, at least two weeks before China officially shared the virus’ genome sequence with the WHO on 11 January 2020.

Divulging this information immediately could have had a decisive impact, potentially ensuring swifter international containment efforts and helping the global medical community to understand how the virus spreads and to draft containment and treatment plans sooner. This report is in keeping with the continual lack of transparency that has characterised China’s actions during and after the pandemic.
In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission believe that these reports are accurate? If so, how will they change overall assessments of China’s initial response to the COVID pandemic?
In the light of the above reports, is the Commission planning to take any specific steps in respect of the People’s Republic of China?
answer: The World Health Organisation (WHO) published reports on the public health investigations done in the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic (1). The WHO officially asked China again in 2023 to share further information. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control collaborates with the China Centre of Disease Control.

Under the memorandum of understanding between both Centres, new evidence can be brought forward and discussed. The Commission would like to clarify that sequencing results in themselves do not constitute a notifiable event under the International Health Regulations 2005 (2) regarding alert and response.

In accordance with the International Health Regulations 2005, China first notified preliminary information to the WHO on 3 January 2020. China consequently shared its sequencing results with WHO and the global sequencing community on 11 January 2020 (3).
